Michael Carrick was just the latest fall guy for Manchester United’s dysfunctional hierarchy | Jamie Jackson

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1012 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Disastrous decisions and confused appointments have been a constant theme at Old Trafford since Sir Alex Ferguson’s retirement in 2013.
  • For a window into the alarming dysfunction at Manchester United that Michael Carrick failed to manage and caused his sacking, consider the case of Eddie Howe, initially a favourite to succeed the 45-year-old before Mauricio Pochettino’s emergence as the chosen one.
  • In a recent development, the former Newcastle manager had been Jason Wilcox’s choice to take over from Carrick.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disastrous decisions and confused appointments have been a constant theme at Old Trafford since Sir Alex Ferguson’s retirement in 2013.

For a window into the alarming dysfunction at Manchester United that Michael Carrick failed to manage and caused his sacking, consider the case of Eddie Howe, initially a favourite to succeed the 45-year-old before Mauricio Pochettino’s emergence as the chosen one.

In a recent development, the former Newcastle manager had been Jason Wilcox’s choice to take over from Carrick. Howe was also the favoured candidate of Dan Ashworth, Wilcox’s predecessor as United’s director of football, to follow Erik ten Hag after the Dutchman’s sacking in October 2024. Except Wilcox disagreed and Sir Jim Ratcliffe went with Wilcox’s man, Ruben Amorim, and that December Ashworth departed only five months after joining.

At that juncture Wilcox was the technical director. Now he is United’s highest-ranking football executive, the powerbroker. He was able, apparently with a straight face, to recommend to Ratcliffe that Howe, nearly two years after he rejected him, should become United’s eighth permanent No 1 in the 13 and a half years since Sir Alex Ferguson retired.

According to recent reports, if following this is difficult, making sense of it is near impossible. Should London’s West End need a latest farce then look no further than the wacky world of Ratcliffe and the football department he leads, which is also headed up by Omar Berrada, the chief executive, and is proving a disjointed, illogical operation.

Industry observers note that yet if this meant Carrick was dealt a treacherous hand, it is also true that he should have played it better. This, after all, is the job of a football coach: to somehow make wine from water – even if the water is murky, and may need purifying first.

José Mourinho, one of Carrick’s predecessors, from May 2016 to December 2018, revealed how – to a degree. Mourinho stated famously that leading United to second place in 2017-18 (with 81 points, 19 behind Manchester City) was one of his finest achievements. This from a serial winner who broke the United-Arsenal duopoly of the Premier League to take Chelsea to consecutive crowns (2004-05 and 2005-06), and made history in Italy by guiding Inter to the treble in 2009-10.

Mourinho’s billing of that second place was down to having to negotiate a similar shambles, overseen by Ed Woodward, the then executive vice-chair.

The Portuguese’s opening campaign ended with the Carabao Cup and Europa League collected despite, like Carrick, having to deal with a hierarchy convinced that it knew better than the man it hired as the football expert.

In a recent development, here we arrive at a fundamental quality Carrick lacked: an ability to be streetwise when really required. For an example of Mourinho’s nous, rewind to a pre-season tour of America when this correspondent was offered an off-the-record sounding about a player he wanted out of the club but the executive did not.

The manager wanted his message out – that this was a player non grata. Machiavellian or pragmatic? A guess notes Carrick would never dream of employing a similar tactic to achieve the best result for the team. But why not? Mourinho wanted a bad egg gone before the dressing room was stunk out and on-field prospects undermined.

Carrick, in his last month, encountered two of his own malevolents: Lisandro Martínez, a de facto captain who dared to criticise Wilcox’s recruitment after the 2-0 defeat by Atlético Madrid; and Bruno Fernandes, Carrick’s official leader, who betrayed his manager by questioning his tactics after the 4-1 humiliation at Como.

Each crossed a line and were emblematic of a chaotic changing room, a major factor in the dismal run of three wins from 15 games this season, including elimination from the Carabao Cup, and the league return of eight points from 10 matches that has United in the relegation zone.

Fernandes, Martínez and a club run like a banana republic are the next man’s problem, just as Mourinho inherited from Louis van Gaal, who was sacked the day after winning the 2016 FA Cup, the faults at boardroom level embodied by Woodward.

Here we see the recurring problem at United: a new gun is hired and is bequeathed a sorry mess that is impossible to clean up because there is no true will to eradicate it. Why? Because the only real reset of culture would be for Ratcliffe, who owns 29.4%, Wilcox, Berrada and the Glazer family, whose ownership since 2005 has left the club about £1.2bn in debt, to accept they are the problem and depart.

According to recent reports, carrick is a good guy whose adoration of United was returned to him by the support, underlined by the reception he got from the Stretford End after the 3-0 humbling by Bournemouth last month. Yet being a decent man and head coach was not enough.

In elite sport the fine margins are often trumpeted as the difference between triumph and failure. Last season, from mid-January, Carrick worked these his way as Manchester City, Arsenal, Liverpool and Chelsea were defeated and United lost only two of his 17 games as interim head coach.

This season, though, the fall-off was startling – and Carrick was found wanting. Who knows what might have occurred if United were the “best-in-class” organisation Ratcliffe insisted they would be under him. As with the muddled thinking regarding Howe, “worst in class” may be a more apt characterisation.

The agonising, overlong process to decide Carrick should be sacked was the latest illustration. On Monday evening the Guardian broke the news that Wilcox and Berrada would recommend to Ratcliffe that Carrick should be removed. Yet days passed during which Carrick still took training and it emerged the deal for Pochettino was being finalised. A proper functioning organisation would have acted more swiftly and with more style.

This is what the next manager has to grapple with. He may succeed. But the odds are stacked against it owing to the deep structural faults that undermine the modern Manchester United.

  • England held on to beat Spain 3-2 with a backs-to-the-wall finale in the Nations League to finish top of their group.
  • But many observers would have been feeling a sense of deja vu from the World Cup semi-final when England sat back and were beaten by Argentina.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

James Trafford (right) kept Spain out in the latter stages.

England held on to beat Spain 3-2 with a backs-to-the-wall finale in the Nations League to finish top of their group.

But many observers would have been feeling a sense of deja vu from the World Cup semi-final when England sat back and were beaten by Argentina.

So what was different this time? BBC Sport has a look.

First of all the context of the two games was entirely different.

England were 1-0 up against Argentina in the 55th minute on neutral territory in Atlanta - and still had all their players.

Anthony Gordon had put them ahead but Lionel Messi set up Enzo Fernandez and then Lautaro Martinez late on.

But against Spain the best performance of Thomas Tuchel's reign had them 3-0 up through goals from Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White.

Elliot Anderson then fouled Lamine Yamal for a penalty, which Mikel Oyarzabal scored - and that began the siege at a partisan Riyadh Air Metropolitano.

Nico Williams made it 3-2 but Spain could not find an equaliser, thanks in part to England keeper James Trafford.

"Half an hour feels like two hours against a team like this [with 10 men]," Tuchel told ITV afterwards. "That's the way it is. Without the red card we were clear winners.".

60 minutes of perfection, 30 minutes of chaos - an England win for the ages.

England cling on to stun world champions Spain in thriller.

Making defensive subs is fine when it works - but when it does not, boy will a manager hear about it.

In the World Cup last 16, England had been 2-1 up against Mexico in the Azteca when Jarell Quansah was sent off.

Tuchel brought on three defenders for a defender, a midfielder and a forward.

But England won 3-2 and Dan Burn's cameo was the stuff of legend.

However, nine days later with England 1-0 up against Argentina, Tuchel did the same again - three defenders on for a defender, midfielder and forward.

The first of those subs, with Konsa replacing Anthony Gordon, was in the 72nd minute.

And England just sat back until Argentina broke their resistance.

However, against Spain this time, despite England being down to 10 men and facing incessant pressure, Tuchel was not so quick with defensive subs.

Myles Lewis-Skelly, replacing Harry Kane, was the first on after 78 minutes - 15 minutes after Anderson's sending off. And then five minutes later he brought on two more players - but one of them was a striker in Dominic Calvert-Lewin.

Burn replaced fellow defender White in the 89th minute.

"Harry played 78 minutes, Jude [Bellingham] 83 minutes and then just defending and defending, it's tiring," explained Tuchel.

In a recent development, "So we needed fresh energy. I was asked yesterday what happens if there needs to be a critical or crucial substitution. And I said, I feel free enough to take any substitution if I think it is necessary to help the team and to influence the game.

"I feel free enough to do that and I think there was a lot of defending needed. So we just went for some fresh legs.".

Win over world champions Spain is a 'statement' - Tuchel.

England actually faced more of a siege this time than against the Argentines, the stats confirm.

In the final 30 minutes they faced 19 shots from Spain, with seven on target and an expected goals (xG) total of 2.53.

Argentina, in that time, had 10 shots, with four on target and an xG of 1.41.

In terms of passes from England the numbers were similar with 65 against Argentina and 61 against Spain - both times with an accuracy rate of about 64%.

In Thursday's 2-1 win against Croatia, as a comparison, they tried 557 passes with accuracy of 89%.

Recent findings suggest that "For half an hour it was Mexico reloaded and it felt like we were back in the Azteca. We had to overcome 30 minutes which, against Spain, felt like three hours," Tuchel told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"We defended in a 4-4-1," he continued.

"The difficult thing is it's not only a red card, it's a red card, and a goal so that makes a completely new game. Thirty minutes against the world champion feels like three hours. I stated it before in the stadium and wave after wave after wave.".

England were criticised for blowing a 2-1 half-time lead at Wembley in their first Nations League game with Spain.

But on that day their final 30-minute figurers were much better - with only five shots faced and 176 attempted passes with a 90% accuracy.

Industry observers note that so what was different this time? Perhaps the team showed more resilience and unity?

After Spain had pulled one back England's players had a huddle.

"I love the fact the team went into a huddle and if anything the manager's stepped back because he wants to see the player reaction," said ex-England defender Matt Upson on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"I almost think that the trauma from that sending off of Elliot Anderson has almost been a positive thing for England because it's given the team a chance to get together and cope in what is an incredibly difficult situation and come through the other side.

Recent findings suggest that "There was so much going on in this game. England had to suffer and came through the other side.".

Defender and goalscorer White was asked about the huddle after the game.

"Just stay calm, when you're one down it becomes more difficult and things change so it was all about managing that," he noted.

Another factor was the performance of England keeper James Trafford, who made six saves - with four of them coming in the final 12 minutes of the game with the score at 3-2.

He made an incredible double save to deny Fermin Lopez and Lamine Yamal in injury time.

Upson said: "I think that double save was the moment for Spain and Trafford had the answers.".

Who swaggered around like he owned the place? Spain v England ratings.

Former England and Chelsea star Joe Cole has highlighted the vital importance of protecting grassroots pitches across the capital, warning "you can’t produce any footballers without football pitches.".

The 45-year-old enjoyed an illustrious playing career, which included three Premier League titles at Stamford Bridge and 56 caps for the Three Lions, and London’s local playing fields played a pivotal role in shaping his journey to the top.

Recent findings suggest that established in 1890, the charity works to safeguard the capital’s green spaces, inspiring future generations to follow in the footsteps of sporting greats. Speaking exclusively to FourFourTwo, Cole admitted the nomination means a great deal to him.

"London and football are two of the things most dearest to my heart," Cole said. "I’m a London kid. I was born in Camden Town, and obviously football is my passion, so the two things together make perfect sense, and they do a great job there.

"We need to protect the green space, not just for football, but for every sport, for kids to play, particularly in London. We have a rich history of producing footballers. You can’t produce any footballers without football pitches – whether that be five-a-side, seven-a-side, 11-a-side, cricket pitches, anything for young people to go out and be active. It’s about keeping them off the developers and making sure there’s room for kids to play.".

Renowned throughout his career for his street-footballer flair and close control, Cole honed his trademark skills growing up in north London during the 1980s, making the most of whatever space was available.

"I lived in a ground-floor flat with a tiny garden, so London was my back garden," Cole recalled. "There were no boundaries. There was a bit of grass right outside my house, a wall, and over the back end there was a little concrete seven-a-side pitch.

As he passes Kenny Dalglish’s appearance total, it is notable to remember that it is the left-back’s journey that sets him apart.

Andy Robertson may not be Scotland’s greatest player, but he is indisputably their finest captain. It counts as sacrilege, even to generations who have watched Kenny Dalglish only on YouTube, to reputationally place Robertson above the Liverpool hero on the basis of a cap haul that will reach 103 in St Gallen on Monday. Dalglish’s international career ended at 102 and the curious events that meant he missed the 1986 World Cup.

There is no requirement to compare a left-back in 2026 to a forward from decades earlier. Dalglish and Robertson are men in different positions in essentially a different sport. Instead, Robertson’s march to the top of the cap pile gives cause to laud his contribution.

Those within the Scotland setup regard Robertson as the glue who holds the scene together, a decorated footballer who treats everybody the same and carries out an abundance of unseen work to make this team better. Robertson has routinely paid for squad nights from his own pocket.

According to recent reports, the 32-year-old is as dedicated to overall environment as he is to his craft. Under Robertson’s on-field guidance, Scotland have morphed from international also-rans to serial tournament participants.

Left-backs are rarely the recipients of praise. When of the status of Robertson they do, however, receive criticism when a team struggle. He has carried the heaviest load while probably unable to celebrate the highs in an appropriate manner.

Robertson’s journey sets him apart and not only from Dalglish. By March 2014, when Robertson made his debut as a 67th-minute substitute in a friendly in Warsaw, he had been rejected by Celtic’s youth system, reset his career at Queen’s Park and turned heads in Dundee United colours. Hull would come next.

Sources indicate that “He counts as one of my best-ever signings,” indicates Steve Bruce, who took Robertson to Humberside. “I still remember him holding his parents’ hands when he came down.

Sources indicate that “He could run like the wind and had such a lovely left foot. We wanted to try and sign the best young players and thought he might get a few games due to injuries but Andy went into the side and never came out, which is testament to him. I’m absolutely delighted for him.”.

Recent findings suggest that robertson and Phil Bardsley replaced Alan Hutton and Barry Bannan in Poland. “He was a young boy who played with so much freedom,” Hutton says. “He had energy and aggression to go up and down the pitch all day long, he would shell crosses into the box at 100mph. For one so young, he was also amazingly good at one v one defending. I got to 50 caps. I remember thinking there would be no chance of anybody reaching 100.”.

Alex McLeish, who handed Robertson the Scotland captaincy in 2018, jokes about the possible impact on Dalglish. “Kenny will want to make a comeback,” he says. “No, he will be absolutely delighted for Andy. It tells you so much about Andy’s character that someone like Kenny Dalglish is so fond of him.

“It felt to me like a fresh era. We were rebuilding and Andy seemed to make the most sense as being at the forefront of that. I’m pretty sure anyone else would have made the same decision. A fantastic player with a great attitude and very well liked by all his teammates. He was a natural captain. He demands high levels without being someone to blast people. He is a hard bugger; if he talks, people shut up and listen.

“When I told him [he was captain], I still remember how his eyes lit up. He loved hearing that. He gave me such a great big smile and said how honoured he would be to captain the country.”.

McLeish underplays the value of his decision. Robertson has worn the armband 80 times. McLeish could easily, for example, have handed it to Kieran Tierney, Callum McGregor or John McGinn. McLeish’s faith in Robertson and convincing of Scott McTominay to commit to Scotland were huge and lasting contributions.

It has been revealed that robertson’s career could easily have followed an alternative path. The Scottish game is laced with players released by major clubs who spend years lurching about in its nether regions. Blair Spittal, who played with Robertson at Queen’s Park and Dundee United, believes there may be a broader lesson here. “I’m not saying every player could do the same as Andy, but within the pyramid of Scottish football there are definitely players who just need an opportunity and someone to show their belief,” he claims.

In a recent development, “Queen’s Park at the time was a great environment for that. We were then very lucky at Dundee United to have a manager [Jackie McNamara] who believed in young players. Andy took everything in his stride. Nothing ever fazed him.”.

He has made instant impressions everywhere. John Rankin was a senior player at Dundee United as Robertson elevated his reputation. He recalls a pre-season friendly at Union Berlin, when he first clapped eyes on someone who would be a Champions League winner within six years. “Who is this?” Rankin noted while watching from the stand. “On his first day at the training ground, Andy bypassed the first‑team dressing room to get changed with the youth team. He was so unassuming, no entitlement about him at all.

Recent findings suggest that “He knew what he wanted to do. On the pitch it was a case of: ‘Get out my road, I’m coming through.’ Off the pitch he was such a humble guy, who knew his life was built on the hard work of his parents. He had hunger to be the best player in every single session. It was never about being flash, it was about working his way to the top.”.

It has been revealed that during a game at Motherwell, with United 3-0 up, Rankin warned teammates to remain compact. Next came a marauding Robertson, who cracked home a fourth before Rankin chastised him for not following orders. “But I scored, didn’t I?” came the retort.

Sources indicate that jordan Henderson and James Milner have been hugely influential in shaping how Robertson deals with others. Robertson did not want Steve Clarke to call time on his Scotland managerial career in June, but during an emotional meeting in Charlotte it was clear the latter’s mind was made up. Clarke would not have returned to Hampden Park four months later but for Robertson, who was receiving recognition for 100 caps.

It is fortunate Dalglish is not protective of his record. McGinn entered this international break with 93 caps. Ryan Christie and McTominay have an outside chance of reaching 102. Billy Gilmour is 25, but hit 50 caps in October. “It’s not about now holding on to the record for ever,” Robertson says. “That’s not really me.”.

According to recent reports, modesty. A consistent and endearing Robertson trait. Whenever this international career for the ages ends, he will be a monumental loss.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, the Imagination Scientist: Researching Pretend Beings and their Creators Paige E.
  • When my brother Arnie was about four years old, he began chatting about an imaginary and invisible companion named Embley, who seemingly travelled with him everywhere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Projecting thoughts and feelings onto imagined friends helps children to develop their social skills.Credit: Oscar Wong/Getty.

According to recent reports, the Imagination Scientist: Researching Pretend Beings and their Creators Paige E. Davis Oxford Univ. Press (2026).

When my brother Arnie was about four years old, he began chatting about an imaginary and invisible companion named Embley, who seemingly travelled with him everywhere. During a 1970s epidemic of whooping cough (linked to an unwarranted vaccine-safety scare), Arnie became sick with this braying cough, which kept him home from school for more than six weeks.

Recent findings suggest that embley was the “same size, age and disposition as me”, my brother recalled later, and he offered companionship and “exploration of potential sources of adventure”. Although he could not remember other aspects of Embley’s personality or appearance, my brother did add one pertinent detail: “He was always available.”.

The great rewiring: is social media really behind an epidemic of teenage mental illness?

The great rewiring: is social media really behind an epidemic of teenage mental illness?

I thought of Embley while reading The Imagination Scientist, a deeply researched and highly entertaining look at the world of imaginary companions by developmental psychologist Paige Davis.

In a recent development, it seems that Embley exemplified several features of children’s imaginary friends: he was comforting and constant; he played with my brother; and he perhaps enabled him to process fear and cope with the stress of a serious illness. He might also have insulated my brother from loneliness while his older siblings were at school. Most importantly, my brother himself created Embley’s mind.

According to recent reports, that last characteristic of an imaginary friend is key, asserts Davis. “My theory is that the most key aspect of the imaginary creature, no matter whether it is seen or unseen, lies in the creation of its mind by the child,” she writes. “To have an invisible friend or personified object considered as an imaginary companion, the child must create, conceptualize, and interact with the separate and distinct mind.”.

Davis opens a wardrobe door, Narnia-style, into a whimsical world inhabited by imaginary companions — some invisible, others personified in a doll or stuffed toy. Up to 65% of children up to the age of seven have had imaginary companions at some stage, according to research by psychologist Marjorie Taylor. Some imaginary friends disappear at the end of childhood, others continue to accompany their creators into adolescence. But not all made-up playmates are friendly: some are a nuisance and might even pick fights with their creators (or vice versa).

Sources indicate that generally, there’s nothing pathological about creating a pretend friend, Davis contends. On the contrary, the presence of such a pal might fortify the child as they deal with transitions or scary situations. Children do understand the distinction between fantasy friends and real ones, and can grasp this difference as young as three years old. “Imaginary friends are a very common, developmentally appropriate phenomena that occurs in multiple cultures around the world,” Davis writes. They “are not only a healthy form of play, but they can be extremely enjoyable for their creator”.

Imaginary friends can offer a child a sense of protection.Credit: Ian Nolan/Getty.

Industry observers note that they’re also great fun to read about. I laughed aloud as I learnt about some of the “human, non-human, and superhuman” forms that Davis has encountered while interviewing children for her research. “I’ve had blue blobs, yellow birds, and rainbow hair,” she writes, “a fire-boy who erupts like a volcano when he becomes angry” and “a genderless imaginary companion that snacks on lightbulbs”. One little girl had twin imaginary companions, who themselves had made their own imaginary friend, “which I thought was quite meta”, she writes.

In a recent development, davis first began immersing herself in the world of imaginary companions as a PhD student at the University of Durham, UK. I “thought about how much fun it would be to work with children, play, and imagination for a job”, Davis writes. It’s clear that, a decade and a half later, she still derives a delicious glee from listening to the odd observations of children (including her two sons).

It has been revealed that in one of her early studies, Davis and her colleagues looked at the relationship between imaginary companions and “theory of mind”, an umbrella term that involves understanding that other people have emotions, thoughts and ideas, just as we do. Thus, writes Davis, “children with a theory of mind are able to put themselves in another person’s shoes to infer what they may be thinking or feeling.”.

Florian Wirtz scored twice as Germany hit four goals in 18 second-half minutes to thrash the Netherlands 5-0 in Berlin and reach the Nations League quarter-finals as group winners. Germany, the Netherlands and Greece all finished on 11 points in Group A2 after substitute Giorgos Masouras scored in the 69th minute to give Greece a 1-0 win over Serbia at home.

The Dutch advanced as runners-up and Greece finished third while Serbia ended the campaign without a point. It was the Netherlands' ​first ⁠defeat since Xavi Hernandez took charge in August. The Dutch had beaten Greece 7-0 three days earlier and needed a draw in Berlin to win the ⁠group.

Jurgen Klopp’s side entered Monday’s match third in the Group A2 standings and Derry Scherhant scored his first international goal with a stunning top-corner finish to put the hosts in front at the break. Germany then put in a ruthless second half display as Wirtz bagged a brace, while Nico Schlotterbeck and Brajan Gruda also got on the scoresheet to complete a stunning victory.

"We always hope we can give the fans a lot of enjoyment. And we enjoyed it very, very much ourselves, especially in the second half," Wirtz stated.

Donyell Malen had a chance to put the visitors ahead but headed over from close range. Scherhant hit the post at the other end before cutting in from the left in the 41st minute and firing into the top corner for his first international goal. The 24-year-old Freiburg winger grew up ‌five minutes from the Olympiastadion, where he made his ‌Bundesliga debut for Hertha Berlin.

Sources indicate that "What can I say? I don't think it could have gone any better. I couldn't even have dreamed of a better outcome. It's truly unbelievable. I had an incredible time out there and I'm just absolutely delighted," Scherhant noted.

It has been revealed that wirtz doubled the lead on the hour with a left-footed drive from outside the box that went in off the far post. Schlotterbeck headed in Gruda's free kick five minutes later before Gruda set up Wirtz for a close-range finish in the 71st.

Gruda turned in a rebound in the 77th minute after Scherhant struck ​the post.

Sources indicate that germany's fifth goal secured top spot on head-to-head goal difference. ‌.

The Dutch had last trailed by five ⁠goals in an international in 1959, when West Germany beat them 7-0 in ⁠Cologne.
